n:
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Woe [to] those who go down to Egypt for help.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and trust in chariots for they are many.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and in horsemen for they are very strong [or “numerous”].”

*Study note:* See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in {{Isaiah 1:4|1:4}}.

*Study note:* This statement appears to have a sarcastic tone. The royal advisers who are advocating an alliance with Egypt think they are wise, but the Lord possesses wisdom as well and will thwart their efforts.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he does not turn aside [i.e., “retract”] his words”; NIV “does not take back his words.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he will arise against the house of the wicked.”

*Study note:* That is, Egypt.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and against the help of the doers of sin.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will extend”; KJV, ASV, NASB, NCV “stretch out.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “together all of them will come to an end.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “As a lion growls, a young lion over its prey.” In the Hebrew text the opening comparison is completed later in the verse (“so the Lord will come down…”), after a parenthesis describing how fearless the lion is. The present translation divides the verse into three sentences for English stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Though there is summoned against it fullness of shepherds, by their voice it is not terrified, and to their noise it does not respond.”

*Translator's note:* Some prefer to translate the phrase לִצְבֹּא עַל (litsboʾ ʿal) as “fight against,” but the following context pictures the Lord defending, not attacking, Zion.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “just as birds fly.” The words “over a nest” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* The only other occurrence of this verb is in {{Exodus 12:13|Exod 12:13}}, {{Exodus 12:23|23}}, {{Exodus 12:27|27}}, where the Lord “passes over” (i.e., “spares”) the Israelite households as he comes to judge their Egyptian oppressors. The noun פֶּסַח (pesakh, “Passover”) is derived from the verb. The use of the verb in {{Isaiah 31:5|Isa 31:5}} is probably an intentional echo of the Exodus event. As in the days of Moses the Lord will spare his people as he comes to judge their enemies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Return to the one [against] whom the sons of Israel made deep rebellion.” The syntax is awkward here. A preposition is omitted by ellipsis after the verb (see GKC 446 §138.*f*, n. 2), and there is a shift from direct address (note the second plural imperative “return”) to the third person (note “they made deep”). For other examples of abrupt shifts in person in poetic style, see GKC 462 §144.*p*.

*Translator's note:* Or “in that day” (KJV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “reject” (so NIV); NRSV, TEV, CEV, NLT “throw away.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their idols of silver and their idols of gold which your hands made for yourselves [in] sin.” חָטָא (khataʾ, “sin”) is understood as an adverbial accusative of manner. See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:573, n. 4.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Assyria will fall by a sword, not of a man.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and a sword not of humankind will devour him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will flee for himself from before a sword.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rocky cliff” (cf. ASV, NASB “rock”), viewed metaphorically as a place of defense and security.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “His rocky cliff, because of fear, will pass away [i.e., “perish”].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they will be afraid of the flag, his officers.”

*Study note:* The “fire” and “firepot” here symbolize divine judgment, which is heating up like a fire in Jerusalem, waiting to be used against the Assyrians when they attack the city.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will reign according to fairness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will rule according to justice.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a man,” but אִישׁ (ʾish) probably refers here to “each” of the officials mentioned in the previous verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Eyes that see.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text as vocalized reads literally “will not gaze,” but this is contradictory to the context. The verb form should be revocalized as תְּשֹׁעֶינָה (teshoʿenah) from שָׁעַע (shʿaʿa, “be blinded”); see {{Isaiah 6:10|Isa 6:10}}; {{Isaiah 29:9|29:9}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “ears that hear.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the heart of rashness will understand knowledge”; cf. NAB “The flighty will become wise and capable.”

*Translator's note:* Or “foolishness,” in a moral-ethical sense. See {{Isaiah 9:17|9:17}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his heart commits sin”; KJV, ASV “his heart will work iniquity”; NASB “inclines toward wickedness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in order to do [or “so that he does”] what is godless [or “defiled”].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so that he leaves empty the appetite [or “desire”] of the hungry.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the drink of the thirsty he causes to fail.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “as for a deceiver, his implements [or “weapons”] are evil.”

*Translator's note:* Or “he plans evil things”; NIV11 “they make up evil schemes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to ruin the poor with words of falsehood, even when the needy speak what is just.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he upon honorable things stands.”

*Translator's note:* Or “self-assured”; NASB, NRSV “who are at ease.”

*Translator's note:* Or “self-confident”; NAB “overconfident.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “days upon a year.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “olive.” See {{Isaiah 24:13|24:13}}.

*Translator's note:* The imperatival forms in v. {{Isaiah 32:11|11}} are problematic. The first (חִרְדוּ, khiredu, “tremble”) is masculine plural in form, though spoken to a feminine plural addressee (שַׁאֲנַנּוֹת, shaʾanannot, “complacent ones”). The four imperatival forms that follow (רְגָזָה, regazah, “shake with fear”; פְּשֹׁטָה, peshotah, “strip off your clothes”; עֹרָה, ʿorah, “expose yourselves”; and חֲגוֹרָה, khagorah, “put on”) all appear to be lengthened (so-called “emphatic”) masculine singular forms, even though they too appear to be spoken to a feminine plural addressee. GKC 131-32 §48.*i* suggests emending חִרְדוּ (khiredu) to חֲרָדָה (kharadah) and understanding all five imperatives as feminine plural “Aramaized” forms.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has “over mourning breasts.” The reference to “breasts” would make sense in light of v. {{Isaiah 32:11|11}}, which refers to the practice of women baring their breasts as a sign of sorrow (see J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* [NICOT], 1:585). However, one expects the preposition עַל (ʿal) to introduce the source or reason for mourning (see vv. {{Isaiah 32:12|12b-13a}}) and the participle סֹפְדִים (sofedim, “mourning”) seems odd modifying “breasts.” The translation above assumes a twofold emendation: (1) שָׁדַיִם (shadayim, “breasts”) is emended to [ם]שָׂדַי (saday[m], “field,” a term that also appears in {{Isaiah 56:9|Isa 56:9}}). The final mem (ם) would be enclitic in this case, not a plural indicator. (The Hebrew noun שָׂדֶה (sadeh, “field”) forms its plural with an וֹת- [-ot] ending). (2) The plural participle סֹפְדִים is emended to סְפֹדָה (sefodah), a lengthened imperatival form, meaning “mourn.” For an overview of various suggestions that have been made for this difficult line, see Oswalt, 586, n. 12).

*Translator's note:* “Mourn” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. In the Hebrew text vv. {{Isaiah 32:12|12-13}} are one long sentence.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “indeed, over all the houses of joy.” It is not certain if this refers to individual homes or to places where parties and celebrations were held.

*Study note:* This same phrase is used in {{Isaiah 22:2|22:2}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “noisy” (NAB, NIV, NCV).

*Translator's note:* Hebrew עֹפֶל (ʿofel), probably refers here to a specific area within the city of Jerusalem. See *HALOT* 861 s.v. II עֹפֶל.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has בְעַד מְעָרוֹת (veʿad meʿarot). The force of בְעַד, which usually means “behind, through, round about,” or “for the benefit of,” is uncertain here. *HALOT* 616 s.v. *מְעָרָה takes מְעָרוֹת (meʿarot) as a homonym of “cave” and defines it here as “cleared field.” Despite these lexical problems, the general point of the statement seems clear—the city will be uninhabited.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the joy of wild donkeys, a pasture for flocks.”

*Translator's note:* The words “The desolation will continue” refer to the previous context and have been added for smoothness.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “until a spirit is emptied out on us from on high.” The words “this desolation will continue” are supplied in the translation for clarification and stylistic purposes. The verb עָרָה (ʿarah), used here in the Niphal, normally means “lay bare, expose.” The term רוּחַ (ruakh, “spirit”) is often understood here as a reference to the divine spirit (cf. {{Isaiah 44:3|44:3}} and NASB, NIV, CEV, NLT), but it appears here without an article (cf. NRSV “a spirit”), pronominal suffix, or a genitive (such as “of the Lord”). The translation assumes that it carries an impersonal nuance “vivacity, vigor” in this context.

*Translator's note:* The term כַּרְמֶל (karmel) may refer to fertile land, an orchard, a garden of vines, a plantation of trees, or fresh grain. The dictionaries may subdivide these meaning under homonyms (see BDB 502, *NIDOTTE* 718, *HALOT* 499, *The Concise DCH*, 183). The picture of transformation is clearer when it is understood that a מִדְבָּר (midbar, “wilderness”) is an area that does not receive enough rainfall to support trees.

*Study note:* The same statement appears in {{Isaiah 29:17|29:17b}}, where, in conjunction with the preceding line, it appears to picture a reversal. Here it seems to depict supernatural growth. The desert will blossom into an orchard, and the trees of the orchard will multiply and grow tall, becoming a forest.
*Study note:* This new era of divine blessing will also include a moral/ethical transformation, as justice and fairness fill the land and replace the social injustice so prevalent in Isaiah’s time.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the product of fairness will be peace.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the work of fairness [will be] calmness and security forever.”
*Translator's note:* Or “in safe resting places”; NAB, NRSV “quiet resting places.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [?] when the forest descends.” The form וּבָרַד (uvarad) is often understood as an otherwise unattested denominative verb meaning “to hail” (*HALOT* 154 s.v. I ברד). In this case one might translate, “and it hails when the forest is destroyed” (cf. KJV, ASV, NASB, NIV). Perhaps the text alludes to a powerful wind and hail storm that knocks down limbs and trees. Some prefer to emend the form to וְיָרַד (veyarad), “and it descends,” which provides better, though not perfect, symmetry with the parallel line (cf. NAB). Perhaps וּבָרַד should be dismissed as dittographic. In this case the statement (“when the forest descends”) lacks a finite verb and seems incomplete, but perhaps it is subordinate to v. {{Isaiah 32:20|20}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and in humiliation the city is laid low.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by all the waters.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who set free the foot of the ox and donkey”; NIV “letting your cattle and donkeys range free.”

*Study note:* This verse seems to anticipate a time when fertile land is available to cultivate and crops are so abundant that the farm animals can be allowed to graze freely.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Woe [to] the destroyer.”

*Study note:* In this context “the destroyer” appears to refer collectively to the hostile nations (vv. {{Isaiah 33:3|3-4}}). Assyria would probably have been primary in the minds of the prophet and his audience.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the deceitful one”; NAB, NIV84 “O traitor”; NIV11 “you betrayer”; NRSV “you treacherous one.” In the parallel structure הוֹי (hoy, “woe [to]”) does double duty.

*Text-critical note:* The form in the Hebrew text appears to derive from an otherwise unattested verb נָלָה (nalah). The translation follows the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa in reading ככלתך, a Piel infinitival form from the verbal root כָּלָה (kalah), meaning “finish.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Be their arm each morning.” “Arm” is a symbol for strength. The mem suffixed to the noun has been traditionally understood as a third person suffix, but this is contrary to the context, where the people speak of themselves in the first person. The mem (מ) is probably enclitic with ellipsis of the pronoun, which can be supplied from the context. See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:589, n. 1.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Be] also our deliverance in the time of distress.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the sound of tumult the nations run away.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because of your exaltation the nations scatter.”

*Translator's note:* The pronoun is plural; the statement is addressed to the nations who have stockpiled plunder from their conquests of others.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and your plunder is gathered, the gathering of the locust.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a swarm of locusts swarming on it.”

*Translator's note:* Or “elevated”; NCV, NLT “is very great.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for” (KJV, NASB, NIV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “on high” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV); CEV “in the heavens.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he is the stability of your times.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a rich store of deliverance, wisdom, and knowledge.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fear of the Lord, it is his treasure.”

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew word is unknown. Proposals include “heroes” (cf. KJV, ASV “valiant ones”; NASB, NIV “brave men”); “priests,” “residents [of Jerusalem].” The present translation assumes that the term is synonymous with “messengers of peace,” with which it corresponds in the parallel structure of the verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “messengers of peace,” apparently those responsible for negotiating the agreements that have been broken (see v. {{Isaiah 33:8|8}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “desolate” (NAB, NASB); NIV, NRSV, NLT “deserted.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one passing by on the road ceases.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one breaks a treaty”; NAB “Covenants are broken.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “he despises cities.” The term עָרִים (ʿarim, “cities”) probably needs to be emended to an original עֵדִים (ʿedim, “[legal] witnesses”), a reading that is preserved in the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa. Confusion of dalet (ד) and resh (ר) is a well-attested scribal error.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he does not regard human beings.”

*Translator's note:* Or “earth” (KJV); NAB “the country.”

*Translator's note:* Or “mourns” (BDB 5 s.v. I אָבַל). *HALOT* 6-7 lists homonyms I אבל (“mourn”) and II אבל (“dry up”). They propose the second here on the basis of parallelism. See {{Isaiah 24:4|24:4}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Lebanon is ashamed.” The Hiphil is exhibitive, expressing the idea, “exhibits shame.” In this context the statement alludes to the withering of vegetation.

*Study note:* *Sharon* was a fertile plain along the Mediterranean coast. See {{Isaiah 35:2|35:2}}.

*Translator's note:* The rift valley (עֲרָבָה, ʿaravah) is a geographic feature extending from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. Especially in the vicinity of the Dead Sea and then ranging southward, it is very dry with little vegetation.

*Study note:* Both of these areas were known for their trees and vegetation. See {{Isaiah 2:13|2:13}}; {{Isaiah 35:2|35:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “shake off [their leaves]” (so ASV, NRSV); NAB “are stripped bare.”
*Translator's note:* Or “lift myself up” (KJV); NLT “show my power and might.”

*Translator's note:* The second person verb and pronominal forms in this verse are plural. The hostile nations are the addressed, as the next verse makes clear.

*Study note:* The hostile nations’ plans to destroy God’s people will come to nothing; their hostility will end up being self-destructive.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will be a burning to lime.” See {{Amos 2:1|Amos 2:1}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “trembling” (ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV); NLT “shake with fear.”

*Translator's note:* Or “the defiled”; TEV “The sinful people of Zion”; NLT “The sinners in Jerusalem.”

*Translator's note:* The words “they say” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* Or “perpetual”; or “everlasting” (KJV, ASV, NAB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “walks” (so NASB, NIV).

*Translator's note:* Or, possibly, “justly”; NAB “who practices virtue.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[who] shakes off his hands from grabbing hold of a bribe.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[who] shuts his ear from listening to bloodshed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[who] closes his eyes from seeing evil.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he [in the] exalted places will live.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mountain strongholds, cliffs [will be] his elevated place.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your eyes will see a king in his beauty”; NIV, NRSV “the king.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a land of distances,” i.e., an extensive land.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your heart will meditate on terror.”

*Translator's note:* The words “and you will ask yourselves” are supplied in the translation for clarification and stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* The people refer to various Assyrian officials who were responsible for determining the amount of taxation or tribute Judah must pay to the Assyrian king.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew form נוֹעָז (noʿaz) is a Niphal participle derived from יָעַז (yaʿaz, an otherwise unattested verb) or from עָזָז (ʿazaz, “be strong,” unattested elsewhere in the Niphal). Some prefer to emend the form to לוֹעֵז (loʿez) which occurs in {{Psalm 114:1|Ps 114:1}} with the meaning “speak a foreign language.” See *HALOT* 809 s.v. עזז, 533 s.v. לעז. In this case, one might translate “people who speak a foreign language.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a people too deep of lip to hear.” The phrase “deep of lip” must be an idiom meaning “lips that speak words that are unfathomable [i.e., incomprehensible].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “derision of tongue there is no understanding.” The Niphal of לָעַג (laʿag) occurs only here. In the Qal and Hiphil the verb means “to deride, mock.” A related noun is used in {{Isaiah 28:11|28:11}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your eyes” (so NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* Or “that does not travel”; NASB “which shall not be folded.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “But there [as] a mighty one [will be] the Lord for us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a place of rivers, streams wide of hands [i.e., on both sides].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a ship of rowing will not go into it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and a mighty ship will not pass through it.”

*Translator's note:* The words “though at this time” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The first half of the verse is addressed to Judah and contrasts the nation’s present weakness with its future prosperity. Judah is compared to a ship that is incapable of sailing.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they do not fasten the base of their mast.” On כֵּן (ken, “base”) see BDB 487 s.v. III כֵּן and *HALOT* 483 s.v. III כֵּן.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “flag.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “then there will be divided up loot of plunder [in] abundance.”

*Study note:* Judah’s victory over its enemies will be so thorough there will be more than enough plunder for everyone, even slow-moving lame men who would normally get left out in the rush to gather the loot.
*Translator's note:* The words “of Zion” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the world and its offspring”; NASB “the world and all that springs from it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will be cast aside”; NASB, NIV “thrown out.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[as for] their corpses, their stench will arise.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hills will dissolve from their blood.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and all the host of heaven will rot.” The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa inserts “and the valleys will be split open,” but this reading may be influenced by {{Micah 1:4|Mic 1:4}}. On the other hand, the statement, if original, could have been omitted by homoioarcton, a scribe’s eye jumping from the conjunction prefixed to “the valleys” to the conjunction prefixed to the verb “rot.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the withering of a leaf from a vine, and like the withering from a fig tree.”

*Translator's note:* The words “he says” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The Lord speaks at this point.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “indeed [or “for”] my sword is drenched in the heavens.” The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has תראה (“[my sword] appeared [in the heavens]”), but this is apparently an attempt to make sense out of a difficult metaphor. Cf. NIV “My sword has drunk its fill in the heavens.”

*Study note:* In v. {{Isaiah 34:4|4}} the “host of the heaven” refers to the heavenly luminaries (stars and planets, see, among others, {{Deuteronomy 4:19|Deut 4:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:3|17:3}}; {{2 Kings 17:16|2 Kgs 17:16}}; {{2 Kings 21:3|21:3}}, {{2 Kings 21:5|5}}; {{2 Kings 23:4|23:4-5}}; 2 Chr 33:3, 5) that populate the divine/heavenly assembly in mythological and prescientific Israelite thought (see {{Job 38:7|Job 38:7}}; {{Isaiah 14:13|Isa 14:13}}). As in {{Isaiah 24:21|24:21}}, they are viewed here as opposing God and being defeated in battle.

*Study note:* Edom is mentioned here as epitomizing the hostile nations that oppose God.

*Translator's note:* The verb is a rare Hotpaal passive form. See GKC 150 §54.*h*.

*Translator's note:* The words “it drips” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* The words “and is covered” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for there is a sacrifice to the Lord.”

*Study note:* The Lord’s judgment of Edom is compared to a bloody sacrificial scene.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “great” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will go down”; NAB “shall be struck down.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and bulls along with strong ones.” Perhaps this refers to the leaders.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for a day of vengeance [is] for the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a year of repayment for the strife of Zion.” The translation assumes that רִיב (riv) refers to Edom’s hostility toward Zion. Another option is to understand רִיב (riv) as referring to the Lord’s taking up Zion’s cause. In this case one might translate, “a time when he will repay Edom and vindicate Zion.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “her”; the referent (Edom) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* קָאַת (qaʾat) refers to some type of bird (cf. Lev 11:18; {{Deuteronomy 14:17|Deut 14:17}}) that was typically found near ruins (see Zeph 2:14). קִפּוֹד (qippod) may also refer to a type of bird (NAB “hoot owl”; NIV “screech owl”; TEV “ravens”), but some have suggested a rodent may be in view (cf. NCV “small animals”; ASV “porcupine”; NASB, NRSV “hedgehog”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will possess it” (so NIV).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has יַנְשׁוֹף וְעֹרֵב (yanshof veʿorev). Both the יַנְשׁוֹף (“owl”; see Lev 11:17; {{Deuteronomy 14:16|Deut 14:16}}) and עֹרֵב (“raven”; Lev 11:15; {{Deuteronomy 14:14|Deut 14:14}}) were types of wild birds.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stones,” i.e., the stones used in a plumb bob.

*Study note:* The metaphor in v. {{Isaiah 34:11|11b}} emphasizes that God has carefully planned Edom’s demise.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will be nothing”; NCV, TEV, NLT “will all be gone.”

*Translator's note:* The words “will grow” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and she will be a settlement for wild dogs, a dwelling place for ostriches.” The translation assumes an emendation of חָצִיר (khatsir, “grass”) to חָצֵר (khatser, “settlement”). One of the Qumran scrolls of Isaiah (1QIsaa) supports this emendation (cf. *HALOT* 344 s.v. II חָצִיר)

*Study note:* Most translations render this as “desert” (KJV, NASB, ESV, NRSV, NIV11, HCSB), “wilderness” (NIV84), or “wasteland” (NLV). The rift valley (עֲרָבָה, ʿaravah), which extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba, is quite arid and desert-like in the areas near the Dead Sea and southward (see the note at {{Numbers 22:1|Num 22:1}}). But the point here has more to do with preparation for a royal visit. To come to Jerusalem from the east requires coming through the rift valley (or Jordan Valley). Thematically, God is typically portrayed as coming to Israel from the east. Similarly in the Gospel accounts Jesus approaches Jerusalem from the east.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and all his loyalty.” The antecedent of the third masculine suffix is בָּשָׂר (basar, “flesh”), which refers collectively to mankind. The normal meaning of חֶסֶד (“faithfulness, loyalty, devotion”) fits very well in the argument. Human beings and their faithfulness (verbal expressions of faithfulness are specifically in view; cf. NRSV “constancy”) are short-lived and unreliable, in stark contrast to the decrees and promises of the eternal God.

*Translator's note:* The first two words of the verse (הַמְסֻכָּן תְּרוּמָה, hamesukkan terumah) are problematic. Some take מְסֻכָּן as an otherwise unattested Pual participle from סָכַן (sakhan, “be poor”) and translate “the one who is impoverished.” תְּרוּמָה (terumah, “contribution”) can then be taken as an adverbial accusative, “with respect to a contribution,” and the entire line translated, “the one who is too impoverished for such a contribution [i.e., the metal idol of v. {{Isaiah 40:19|19}}?] selects wood that will not rot.” However, מְסֻכָּן is probably the name of a tree used in idol manufacturing (cognate with Akkadian musukkanu, cf. H. R. Cohen, *Biblical Hapax Legomena* [SBLDS], 133). מְסֻכָּן may be a scribal interpretive addition attempting to specify עֵץ (ʿets) or עֵץ may be a scribal attempt to categorize מְסֻכָּן. How an idol constitutes a תְּרוּמָה (“contribution”) is not entirely clear.

*Study note:* Exiled Israel’s complaint (v. {{Isaiah 40:27|27}}) implies that God might be limited in some way. Perhaps he, like so many of the pagan gods, has died. But v. {{Isaiah 40:28|28}} affirms that he is not limited temporally or spatially nor are his power and wisdom restricted in any way.
